brief.interpretation: A single launch-announcement email to cold, not-yet-buyers in the selected ops/no-code segment. I interpret “launch” as announcing Tally’s availability as the form front end for a new automation, not as announcing a newly released webhook feature.
brief.reader:
Selected audience: The ops or no-code person on a small team whose intake form is step one of an automation nobody owns.
Research context describes some members of this market, not this recipient's installed tools or experiences. Follow the campaign request when it scopes the job.
Observed situation (inferred; check applicability): Operations and no-code builders at small teams and automation agencies who already run Make, Zapier or n8n scenarios and read webhook documentation before choosing a form tool
brief.reader_segment: The ops or no-code person on a small team whose intake form is step one of an automation nobody owns
brief.promise: Tally can be the form front end for an ops workflow: new submissions can trigger Make, Zapier, or n8n, and webhook access is free to every Tally user.
brief.orientation: Tally is an online form builder that can push new submissions into the automation workflows an ops or no-code builder already knows how to run.
brief.arc: Announce Tally, connect the launch to the reader’s form-to-automation job, explain the documented webhook mechanism and free access, then invite one bounded first step: create the form before deciding whether to wire it into a workflow.
brief.sequence_rationale: There is only one email, so it must carry the complete launch case without assuming the reader has already tried Tally or experienced a specific failure. The argument leads with the relevant workflow topology, not an unsupported promise about mapping, validation, redirects, replay, or delivery-history details. The CTA asks the reader to create the form half of the workflow; it explicitly leaves downstream behavior for a later configured test because the supplied evidence does not provide a pre-signup preview of that behavior.

emails.job: Make the launch relevant to an experienced ops or no-code reader and earn creation of a first form as the bounded first evaluation step.
emails.single_idea: Tally is now available as a form front end for automations: it can push new submissions into workflows built with Make, Zapier, or n8n, and the webhook route is free to use.
emails.felt_need: After a Tally form submits to a webhook, the respondent cannot be reliably redirected or shown a conditional response from the automation tool; the connection appears to be lost once the platform returns its own 'accepted' acknowledgement.
emails.status_quo: Builders are advised to use the generic Webhook trigger module instead of the native Tally app module, because the native module simplifies the payload in a way that complicates handling it downstream.
emails.mechanism: Once a Tally form is connected through a webhook, a new submission can trigger Make, Zapier, or n8n and continue to a CRM, billing tool, internal database, or messaging app. The submission is pushed when it arrives rather than waiting for polling or a CSV export, and webhook access is available free to all Tally users.

alternative_arguments.single_idea: The launch is also a chance to stop treating response volume as a reason to delay trying a new form tool: Tally offers unlimited forms and submissions free within its fair usage guidelines.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: After a Tally form submits to a webhook, the respondent cannot be reliably redirected or shown a conditional response from the automation tool; the connection appears to be lost once the platform returns its own 'accepted' acknowledgement.
alternative_arguments.status_quo: Builders are advised to use the generic Webhook trigger module instead of the native Tally app module, because the native module simplifies the payload in a way that complicates handling it downstream.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: Tally’s free offer covers unlimited forms and submissions, subject to its fair usage guidelines, so the reader can begin with a real form without first selecting a paid tier.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: assumes a serious form evaluation will quickly run into response or form-count limits. After: sees that Tally can be tried on the strength of the form itself before a paid-plan decision, while understanding that fair usage still applies.
must_not_say: Do not describe free usage as unconditional; always retain the fair usage qualification.
Do not claim the create step proves webhook delivery, field mapping, redirect behavior, validation, or production reliability.
Do not introduce paid-plan prices or features; they are unnecessary to this proposition.
Do not claim Tally is the only free or unlimited option.
alternative_arguments.objection: “Free” usually means I will hit a form or submission cap before the workflow becomes useful.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether Tally is worth using for the form at the front of an upcoming workflow before considering a paid plan.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The reader can begin creating the form under an offer that includes unlimited forms and submissions within fair usage guidelines.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: Creating the form does not test webhook payloads, downstream mappings, redirects, validation rules, or production delivery behavior.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Make the launch concrete through the unlimited-free offer, while avoiding generic “big news” language or unsupported exclusivity.

emails.belief_shift: Before: sees the launch as another general-purpose form builder. After: understands that Tally can sit at the start of the automation topology they already use, with free webhook access, and that the sensible first decision is whether the form itself is worth wiring up.
must_not_say: Do not claim Tally’s webhook response can redirect a respondent or display an automation-generated conditional response.
Do not claim Tally fixes field-level mapping failures, including a missing email value in Airtable.
Do not claim an instant trigger processes historical submissions or that a successfully delivered submission can be replayed.
Do not claim Tally resolves multiple-choice IDs into readable labels; P2 is unsupported.
Do not claim Tally validates typos, blank fields, or every bad CRM record before write-through.
Do not describe what endpoint-response details the delivery-history view exposes or make the CTA depend on seeing that view.
Do not imply that creating a form completes or proves the automation; an endpoint must still be configured and tested with a new submission.
Do not promise no setup, flawless delivery, or end-to-end reliability.
Do not add the full feature list, security posture, customer count, paid-plan pricing, or broad integration catalog.
Do not use the unlimited-forms-and-submissions proposition in this version; reserve it for the complete alternative argument.
emails.objection: I do not want to pay for a form tool just to find out whether its webhook route belongs in my workflow.
emails.tone: Warm, casual, and matter-of-fact—like a trusted builder sharing a useful new option, with short sentences and no launch-day hype.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether a Tally form is worth wiring into the next automation this reader builds or replaces.
emails.next_step_value: The reader can start the form that would sit before a Make, Zapier, or n8n workflow, while knowing the webhook route itself is available free.
emails.next_step_limit: Creating the form does not demonstrate webhook delivery, payload shape, field mapping, respondent redirects, historical-submission behavior, or the downstream result; those require configuring an endpoint and sending a new test submission.
emails.subject_strategy: Present the launch as immediately relevant to form-triggered automation, using the free webhook fact to remove evaluation friction rather than relying on vague novelty or hype.

brief.voice_notes: Write as Team Tally: plainspoken, confident, and lightly irreverent. Keep the technical language familiar to a solution-aware no-code reader, but do not turn the announcement into documentation. Use “free” precisely and avoid superlatives.

allowed_claims: Webhooks are available for free to all Tally users.
When a Tally form is submitted, a notification containing the response data is sent to the configured URL in JSON format via a POST request.
Tally webhook endpoints have a 10-second timeout to process and respond to a new submission.
Tally webhook requests can include a Tally-Signature header containing a SHA256 cryptographic hash of the payload for verification.
Tally supports connecting unlimited webhook URLs, which can be paused via a toggle.
If a webhook delivery fails, Tally retries after 5 minutes, then 30 minutes, then 1 hour, then 6 hours, then 1 day.
If all retries fail, Tally sends a one-time email to the form owner and creator with the reason and a link to fix it.
Webhooks created via an integration can only be removed from within that integration.
Tally offers integrations with Zapier, Make, Pipedream, and Integrately for syncing form submissions.
A webhook lets you send every form submission as structured JSON to any HTTP endpoint in real time.
Instead of polling the Tally API or exporting CSVs, webhooks push data the moment a form is submitted.
A Tally form can trigger automation platforms like Make, Zapier, or n8n, which then route the data to CRMs, billing tools, internal databases, or messaging apps.
Tally can sign each webhook request with a SHA256 signature so you can verify that the payload really came from Tally before you process it.
You can list delivery events, inspect responses and retry failed webhook attempts, which makes production workflows much easier to monitor and debug.
Each Tally submission includes a submissionPdfUrl, a generated PDF of the response.
Each Tally submission includes a submissionPreviewUrl, a shareable preview link to the response.
Tally provides unlimited forms, submissions, and everything needed to create forms and surveys all free of charge as long as users stay within Tally's fair usage guidelines.
Tally provides API access to programmatically create, update or delete forms and submissions.
Tally uses reCAPTCHA to protect forms from spam and bots.
Tally can prevent duplicate submissions by allowing only one submission based on a unique identifier.
Tally can send form submissions to Airtable.
Tally Business costs $89/month or $890/year (2 months off)
Tally Business can verify email addresses from form respondents, improving data reliability
Tally offers unlimited forms and submissions completely free, within fair usage guidelines
Make uses Tally
Free plan includes redirect on completion
Tally supports conditional logic to build dynamic forms that show/hide blocks, branch, or calculate values.
Tally supports hidden fields, passing data via URL parameters including UTM parameters or personal data.
Tally can redirect respondents to another web page on completion.
unresolved_objections: Can the automation decide what the respondent sees after they submit?
Does the webhook payload carry the human-readable label for choice options alongside the option id, and is there documented guidance for resolving one from the other?
